selected cluster at the second stage. Environmental examples include selecting
watersheds and then stream reaches within them, or selecting lakes and then
locations within them.

The clusters are the primary sampling units (PSUs), and the units sampled
within them are the secondary sampling units (SSUs). First estimate each
selected PSU's total from its sampled SSUs, then weight those estimated
totals to represent all PSUs in the population. Variance must account for
both which PSUs are selected and which SSUs are selected within them. If every unit in each selected cluster is observed, the design is instead
a single-stage cluster sample: the selected cluster totals are known
exactly, and sampling uncertainty comes only from selecting clusters.

Use $i,j$ for PSUs (clusters) and $k,l$ for elements within a PSU. Let $U_I$
and $\mathcal P$ be the population and sample of PSUs, of sizes $N_I$ and $n_I$;
let $U_i$ and $\mathcal K_i$ be the population and sample of elements in PSU $i$.
In the two-stage notation of @sarndal1992model, write
$\pi_{Ii}$ and $\pi_{Iij}$ for first-stage inclusion probabilities and
$\pi_{k\mid i}$ and $\pi_{kl\mid i}$ for conditional second-stage probabilities.
Then $d_{Ii}=1/\pi_{Ii}$, $d_{k\mid i}=1/\pi_{k\mid i}$, and the combined
weight is $d_{ik}=d_{Ii}d_{k\mid i}$. Assume that second-stage samples are independent across PSUs and that the
sampling design within PSU $i$ does not depend on which other PSUs were
selected.

### The Standard Two-Stage Estimator {#sec:core-twostage-standard}

Under the second-stage independence assumptions above, let
$$
t_i=\sum_{k\in U_i}y_{ik},\qquad
\widehat t_i=\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}d_{k\mid i}y_{ik},\qquad
E_2(\widehat t_i)=t_i,\qquad V_i=V_2(\widehat t_i).
$$
The overall HT estimator is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:twostage-total}
\hat\tau = \sum_{i\in \mathcal P}d_{Ii}\widehat t_i
          = \sum_{i\in \mathcal P}\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}d_{ik}y_{ik}.
\end{equation}
Conditionally on $\mathcal P$, independence of second-stage samples gives
$$
E_2(\hat\tau\mid \mathcal P)=\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}d_{Ii}t_i,
\qquad V_2(\hat\tau\mid \mathcal P)=\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}d_{Ii}^2V_i.
$$
Apply the law of total variance, writing
$\Delta_{Iij}=\pi_{Iij}-\pi_{Ii}\pi_{Ij}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
V(\hat\tau)
 &= \underbrace{V_1\{E_2(\hat\tau\mid \mathcal P)\}}_{\text{between-PSU variation}}
   +\underbrace{E_1\{V_2(\hat\tau\mid \mathcal P)\}}_{\text{within-PSU variation}}\\
 &= \sum_{i,j\in U_I}\Delta_{Iij}d_{Ii}t_i d_{Ij}t_j
    +\sum_{i\in U_I}\pi_{Ii}d_{Ii}^2V_i\\
 &= \sum_{i,j\in U_I}\Delta_{Iij}d_{Ii}t_i d_{Ij}t_j
    +\sum_{i\in U_I}d_{Ii}V_i.
\end{aligned}
$$
The last equality uses $\pi_{Ii}d_{Ii}^2=d_{Ii}$.
The first component is the between-PSU variance: uncertainty about which
PSUs are selected, evaluated using their true totals $t_i$. The second is
the within-PSU variance: uncertainty from estimating each selected PSU's
total using a sample of its SSUs, averaged over first-stage selection.
The subscripts 1 and 2 in $E$ and $V$ refer to these first- and second-stage
sampling operations, respectively.

When the relevant joint inclusion probabilities are positive and unbiased
within-PSU estimates $\widehat V_i$ are available, the HT variance estimator is
$$
\widehat V_{HT}(\hat\tau)
=\sum_{i,j\in \mathcal P}\frac{\Delta_{Iij}}{\pi_{Iij}}
  d_{Ii}\widehat t_i d_{Ij}\widehat t_j
 +\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}d_{Ii}\widehat V_i.
$$
The first term already contains second-stage noise through $\widehat t_i$.
Its expectation equals the between-PSU target plus
$\sum_{i\in U_I}(d_{Ii}-1)V_i$: for $i=j$,
$E_2(\widehat t_i^2)=t_i^2+V_i$ and
$\Delta_{Iii}d_{Ii}^2=(d_{Ii}-1)$. The expectation of the added sample term is
$\sum_{i\in U_I}\pi_{Ii}d_{Ii}V_i=\sum_{i\in U_I}V_i$.
Adding these two noise contributions yields $\sum_{i\in U_I}d_{Ii}V_i$,
as required. Thus the first power in this sample correction is tied to
the HT first-stage variance estimator.
We refer to the first sample term as the between-PSU term and the added
sample correction as the within-PSU term. These names identify where each
calculation is performed; the first term does not estimate only the
between-PSU component, because it also contains the second-stage noise
just described.

The same construction applies to domains. Let $\delta_{ik}$ be one if
element $k$ in PSU $i$ belongs to domain $D$, and zero otherwise. For a
domain total, replace $y_{ik}$ with $\delta_{ik}y_{ik}$ in the point and
variance estimators, including when forming each PSU total. Sampled elements
outside the domain contribute zero rather than being removed from the design. 
For a domain mean, define
$$
\widehat N_D=\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}d_{ik}\delta_{ik},\qquad
\widehat{\bar y}_D=
\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}
      d_{ik}\delta_{ik}y_{ik}}{\widehat N_D}.
$$
Use the linearized response
$\psi_{ik}=\delta_{ik}(y_{ik}-\widehat{\bar y}_D)/\widehat N_D$
in place of $y_{ik}$ in the variance calculation. Its complete weighted
element contribution, conditional second-stage contribution, and weighted
PSU total are, respectively,
$$
z_{ik}=d_{ik}\psi_{ik},\qquad
q_{ik}=d_{k\mid i}\psi_{ik}=z_{ik}/d_{Ii},\qquad
U_i=d_{Ii}\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}q_{ik}=\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}z_{ik}.
$$
Thus the between-PSU calculation uses $U_i$ in place of
$d_{Ii}\widehat t_i$, and each within-PSU calculation uses $q_{ik}$ in
place of $d_{k\mid i}y_{ik}$. The factor $1/\widehat N_D$ is already in
these contributions, so no further denominator division is needed.
This gives a linearization approximation to the variance of the ratio,
rather than an exact variance identity for the mean. For a domain
proportion, take $y_{ik}$ to be the indicator of the category of interest.
`survey` supplies the nonlocal variance calculations,
which leverage their single-stage framework.

### The Local Neighborhood Extension {#sec:core-twostage-local}

For a two-stage design, the first-stage (PSU) arguments are `clusterID`,
`weight1`, `xcoord1`, and `ycoord1`. The second-stage (SSU) arguments are
`siteID`, `weight`, `xcoord`, and `ycoord`; `weight` is the conditional
weight given that the PSU was selected. Optional `sweight1` and `sweight`
supply size weights at the corresponding stages. The local calculation
does not apply an SRS finite population correction at either stage;
the population sizes `Ncluster` and `stage1size`, supplied through `fpc`,
are used for nonlocal inference passed to `survey`.

The `vartype = "local"` calculation substitutes local operators
into the HT sample convention above. Denote the first-stage local operator
by $L_I$ and the within-PSU operator by $L_i$. The formula is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:twostage-var}
\widehat V_{local}(\hat\tau)
=L_I(\{d_{Ii}\widehat t_i\}_{i\in \mathcal P})
 +\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}d_{Ii}L_i(\{d_{k\mid i}y_{ik}\}_{k\in \mathcal K_i}).
\end{equation}
The between-PSU term $L_I$ forms neighborhoods among sampled PSUs using
`xcoord1`, `ycoord1`, and first-stage inclusion probabilities. Each PSU is
represented by one observation, $d_{Ii}\widehat t_i$, at its supplied PSU
coordinates. The within-PSU operator $L_i$ forms neighborhoods separately
among the sampled SSUs in PSU $i$, using `xcoord`, `ycoord`, and conditional
second-stage inclusion probabilities. Its variance contribution is then
multiplied by $d_{Ii}$ and summed over sampled PSUs. A PSU containing a
single sampled SSU contributes nothing to this within-PSU term, since no
within-PSU variability can be estimated from one unit.
PSUs with two or three sampled SSUs use the SRS within-PSU operator.
For direct estimation, fewer than four sampled PSUs also triggers an SRS
first-stage calculation. GREG instead uses survey's calibrated-design
variance for the entire estimate if the first-stage local calculation
cannot be formed.

For a domain mean $\widehat{\bar y}_D$, recall that $q_{ik}$ is the conditional
second-stage weighted deviation $d_{k\mid i}\delta_{ik}(y_{ik}-\widehat{\bar y}_D)/\widehat N_D$,
and $U_i=d_{Ii}\sum_{k\in \mathcal K_i}q_{ik}$ adds these deviations within PSU $i$
and includes its first-stage weight. The local variance estimator is
$$
\widehat V_{local}(\widehat{\bar y}_D)
=L_I(\{U_i\}_{i\in \mathcal P})
 +\sum_{i\in \mathcal P}d_{Ii}L_i(\{q_{ik}\}_{k\in \mathcal K_i}).
$$
Under `subset_local = FALSE`, a sampled PSU with no domain members has
$q_{ik}=0$ for every sampled SSU and $U_i=0$, and remains in the
first-stage neighborhoods. Within each PSU, sampled SSUs outside the domain
likewise remain in the second-stage neighborhoods with zero contributions.


### An Inclusion-Probability View {#sec:core-twostage-inclusion}

Stratified and cluster designs can both be viewed as sampling designs over
the individual elements of the population. Their different selection rules
appear in the elements' marginal and joint inclusion probabilities. To see
this without committing to a particular grouping, temporarily use $a,b$ for
individual elements, $U$ for their population, and $s$ for their sample.
Write $I_a$ for the indicator that element $a$ is selected. The HT total and
its exact design variance are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\tau &= \sum_{a\in U}I_a\frac{y_a}{\pi_a}
          = \sum_{a\in s}\frac{y_a}{\pi_a},\\
V(\hat\tau)
 &= \sum_{a\in U}\sum_{b\in U}
    \operatorname{Cov}(I_a,I_b)\frac{y_a}{\pi_a}\frac{y_b}{\pi_b}\\
 &= \sum_{a\in U}\sum_{b\in U}
    (\pi_{ab}-\pi_a\pi_b)\frac{y_a}{\pi_a}\frac{y_b}{\pi_b},
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\pi_{aa}=\pi_a$ and every $\pi_a$ is positive. These expressions
describe the same HT estimator and variance introduced earlier
[@horvitz1952generalization; @sarndal1992model]. Responses are fixed in this
design-based calculation: the covariance is between selection indicators,
not an assumed covariance model for the responses.

For independently sampled strata, elements in different strata satisfy
$\pi_{ab}=\pi_a\pi_b$. Every cross-stratum term in the variance is therefore
zero. Writing $U_h$ for stratum $h$ gives
$$
V(\hat\tau)
=\sum_h\sum_{a,b\in U_h}
  (\pi_{ab}-\pi_a\pi_b)\frac{y_a}{\pi_a}\frac{y_b}{\pi_b}
=\sum_h V(\hat\tau_h).
$$
Selection indicators within a stratum need not be independent. For example,
SRS without replacement of $n_h$ elements from $N_h$ gives, for distinct
$a,b\in U_h$,
$$
\pi_a=\frac{n_h}{N_h},\qquad
\pi_{ab}=\frac{n_h(n_h-1)}{N_h(N_h-1)}.
$$
Thus independence across strata removes the cross-stratum terms while
retaining the dependence induced by sampling within each stratum.

Returning to the PSU and element notation defined above, element $(i,k)$
is observed only if PSU $i$ and then element $k$ within that PSU are selected.
Multiplying the probabilities of these events gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{ik} &= \pi_{Ii}\pi_{k\mid i},\\
\pi_{ik,il} &= \pi_{Ii}\pi_{kl\mid i}, && k\ne l,\\
\pi_{ik,jl} &= \pi_{Iij}\pi_{k\mid i}\pi_{l\mid j}, && i\ne j.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here $\pi_{ik}$ is an element inclusion probability; the capital $I$ in
$\pi_{Ii}$ distinguishes the first-stage PSU probability. Two elements in
the same PSU require just one PSU selection event. Elements in different
PSUs require their joint first-stage selection and two independent
conditional second-stage selections. In particular, for $i\ne j$,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(I_{ik},I_{jl})
=(\pi_{Iij}-\pi_{Ii}\pi_{Ij})\pi_{k\mid i}\pi_{l\mid j}.
$$
Independent second-stage sampling therefore does not generally make
selection indicators in different PSUs independent: they inherit any
dependence in PSU selection.

In a single-stage cluster sample, every element of each selected PSU is
observed. Then $\pi_{k\mid i}=\pi_{kl\mid i}=1$, so
$$
\pi_{ik}=\pi_{Ii},\qquad
\pi_{ik,il}=\pi_{Ii},\qquad
\pi_{ik,jl}=\pi_{Iij}\quad(i\ne j).
$$
Members of a PSU are selected together: $I_{ik}=I_{il}$. At the other
extreme, selecting exactly one element per sampled PSU gives
$\pi_{kl\mid i}=0$ for distinct elements, because they cannot both appear
in the sample. The population variance identity above still holds, but
zero joint inclusion probabilities can prevent an unbiased HT variance
estimator based on observed pairs.

The connection with stratification is also explicit. If every PSU is
selected with certainty, $\pi_{Ii}=\pi_{Iij}=1$, and samples are drawn
independently within PSUs, then cross-PSU selection covariances are zero.
Those PSUs function as strata. In a cluster sample with noncertainty PSU
selection, uncertainty about which PSUs appear must also be included.

## Size Weights {#sec:core-sizeweight}

Sometimes a sampled site stands for an amount of resource rather than for a
count of units. Setting `sizeweight = TRUE` and supplying `sweight` (and
`sweight1` for the first stage of a two-stage design) multiplies the design
weight by a size variable, so that
$$
w_i^{\mathrm{sw}} = w_i \times \texttt{sweight}_i .
$$

An example makes the construction concrete. Suppose lakes are sampled from a
sampling frame of lake centroids (points), a particular lake is selected with
$\pi_i = 0.02$, so $w_i = 50$, and that lake has area 30 hectares. With no
size weight, $\hat\tau$ built from $w_i$ estimates a count: This lake stands
for 50 lakes. With `sweight` set to the lake area, the site's weight becomes
$w_i^{\mathrm{sw}} = 50 \times 30 = 1500$ hectares, and $\hat\tau$ built from
$w_i^{\mathrm{sw}}$ estimates total lake area rather than total lake count.
The same device converts a stream sample from a count of reaches into a total
length by setting `sweight` to reach length. The size weight enters as a multiplicative adjustment to the design weight
before any variance computation begins. It is used wherever $w_i$ appears in
the estimators above, including inside \eqref{eq:local-var}, so no separate
size-weight term appears in any variance formula.

For GREG (`formula` supplied), calibration starts with the product of the
design weight and the size weight. The known population or subpopulation
totals supplied for calibration must therefore be totals of the auxiliary
variables multiplied by the size variable. For example, if lake area is
the size weight, the known intercept total is the total lake area in the
population or subpopulation, rather than the number of lakes. A known
category-indicator total is likewise the total area of lakes in that
category, rather than their count. More generally, for auxiliary variable
$x_i$ and size variable $a_i$, supply $\sum_{i\in U}a_i x_i$ for a population
target or $\sum_{i\in D}a_i x_i$ for a domain target. See
[GREG design features](#sec:greg-extensions) for the constraints and notation.

## The Finite Population Correction {#sec:core-fpc}

The finite population correction is often presented as a separate factor
applied to an otherwise infinite-population variance. It is more usefully
understood as a summary of information that the general variance formula
already contains.

Equation \eqref{eq:ht-var} makes no distinction between finite and infinite
populations. It accounts for the finiteness of the sampling frame through the
inclusion probabilities and the $\Delta_{ij}$. Under SRS without replacement,
the off-diagonal $\Delta_{ij}$ are negative because selecting one unit reduces
the chance of selecting another. Other designs, including cluster samples,
can have positive off-diagonal terms. If joint inclusion probabilities were
known and positive for all pairs, \eqref{eq:ht-var-est}
would need no correction of any kind, since all of the relevant information is
already in $\Delta_{ij}/\pi_{ij}$. The correction appears only when those off-diagonal terms are discarded.
Comparing \eqref{eq:srs-var} with \eqref{eq:wr-var} shows what happens: Under
simple random sampling the entire effect of the off-diagonal $\Delta_{ij}$
collapses into the single scalar $1 - n/N$, so the with-replacement estimator
can be repaired by multiplying it by that factor. This is the familiar finite
population correction, and it can only be factored out because
simple random sampling ensures the correction to be the same
for every pair of units.

The local neighborhood estimator is a variance estimator in the same sense
that \eqref{eq:ht-var-est} is, not a corrected version of \eqref{eq:wr-var}.
It recovers pair information from the realized spatial arrangement rather
than from $\pi_{ij}$, and that information does not collapse into a single
scalar, so there is no finite population correction to factor out of it. It is
also derived for an effectively continuous population, following the extension
of the Horvitz-Thompson framework to continuous universes by
@cordy1993extension.

In practice, `fpc` controls whether population size information is passed
through to `survey`. Supplying it affects the `"SRS"`, `"HT"`, and `"YG"`
variances, and has no effect on $\hat V_{\mathrm{lnb}}$. For a single-stage
design `fpc` gives the sampling-frame size (a count for a finite
point frame, or the applicable length or area for a continuous resource); for a two-stage design `Ncluster` and
`stage1size` give the number of clusters in the sampling frame and the number
of stage-two units within each sampled cluster.

<!-- Retained for further review before publication.
This absence of an explicit FPC is an implementation property, not an
assertion that the local approximation exactly reproduces finite-population
variance. Conditional on the neighborhood weights, an independent,
zero-mean noise component in $z_i$ contributes
$(1-\sum_r \omega_{ri}^2)\operatorname{Var}(z_i)$ to the expected local
estimate, because the column sums of the neighborhood matrix $\Omega$ are one.
The sum runs over neighborhoods containing site $i$. In the neighborhood
stress study, average shares were approximately 0.92 for 15 neighbors and
0.75 for four; these values depend on geometry and weights, not only the
requested neighborhood size. This calculation is separate from the
design's finite population correction and applies at both stages.
Census behavior and this
partial capture of unstructured variation remain limitations. A fallback
to survey's covariance can use supplied finite-population information even
though a successful local calculation does not.
